analysis.one_liner: Bans all logging, mining, drilling, grazing, and road building on federal public lands.
analysis.headline: The bill had one sponsor and no cosponsors, was referred to three House committees and never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made roughly 650 million acres of federal land — national forests, parks, wildlife refuges, and Bureau of Land Management land — off-limits to all commercial use. Tree cutting, logging, mining, drilling, grazing, road building, dams, and motorized recreation would all be banned, with no exceptions. It would also have required federal agencies to inventory every road and stream on those lands, tear out unneeded roads, and let any citizen sue in federal court to enforce the ban, with damages from $5,000 up to 1,000 times the value of whatever was harmed.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who use public lands for hiking, fishing, hunting, and clean water would gain permanent protection for watersheds — the bill's findings note national forests supply 80 percent of America's fresh drinking water. Taxpayers would stop subsidizing commercial extraction of publicly owned timber, minerals, and oil. Rural communities and recreation businesses dependent on intact forests would also gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hikers, anglers, hunters, and water users

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits, with no exceptions, tree cutting, logging, mining, drilling, grazing, road building, dams, and motorized recreation development on all federal public lands, and forbids leasing, selling, or exchanging those lands or their resources [S2][S3].
Requires agencies to inventory all federal public lands by acre, road, river, and stream within two years, and to obliterate and revegetate all non-essential roads within ten years [S2][S3].

Creates citizen-suit enforcement in any federal district court, with mandatory damages of at least $5,000, attorney's fees, injunctions, and asset forfeiture for violators, and waives the federal government's sovereign immunity so it can be sued [S2][S3].

The bill's findings state that national forest lands are the source of 80 percent of America's fresh drinking water, and that surveys indicate at least 80 percent of the public wants these lands protected from harm [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Timber, mining, oil and gas, and grazing interests would lose all access to federal lands, ending decades of commercial operations. Rural communities built around logging, mining, and grazing jobs, and motorized recreation businesses, would bear the economic cost. Federal agencies would face the expense of a nationwide inventory and road removal, and the courts would absorb citizen suits against both companies and the government itself.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber, mining, oil and gas, grazing interests

drawbacks.text: The ban has no exceptions for any purpose — including fire management. The bill declares fires, insects, and disease to be acts of nature with 'no further attempts to correct for such acts of nature' permitted, which would bar fuel-reduction work that forest managers use to reduce wildfire risk to nearby communities and drinking-water watersheds [S2][S3].

Ending all grazing, logging, and mining on federal lands would immediately eliminate existing rural livelihoods in communities built around those uses, with no transition or compensation provisions in the bill [S3].

The enforcement scheme lets any citizen sue with preponderance-of-the-evidence proof, no notice requirement, damages up to 1,000 times the value of the harm, forfeiture of corporate assets, and a full waiver of federal sovereign immunity — a structure that could produce a wave of litigation against both private operators and federal employees [S3].

The bill also bans new dams and water diversions on all federally owned lands including Army Corps of Engineers and TVA lands, which could conflict with existing flood control, hydropower, and water-supply operations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — permanent protection of public lands and watersheds — is popular and substantial, and the bill's own findings argue extraction costs the public more than it returns. But the bill is a maximalist statement version of that goal: zero exceptions, a total ban on grazing and fuel management, sweeping citizen litigation with punitive damages, and no transition for dependent communities. More targeted conservation laws could capture most of the public benefit at far less cost, which is likely why even allies of public-lands protection did not sign on.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by a single sponsor with no cosponsors, referred to three House committees and then to five subcommittees, and sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Cynthia McKinney introduced the Public Lands Forever Wild Act in the House on November 14, 2002 [S1][S2].

It was referred to the Committees on Resources, Agriculture, and Transportation and Infrastructure on the day of introduction, and within a week split among five subcommittees covering energy and minerals, parks, fisheries and wildlife, forests, and agriculture [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in committee when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber, mining, oil and gas, and grazing companies kept their access to federal lands, since nothing changed for them. Nobody who wanted the protection got it.

for.name: Rep. Cynthia McKinney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to three committees; gathered no cosponsors.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Chair with authority to schedule hearings and markups
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup after the bill was referred, along with the Agriculture and Transportation and Infrastructure committees.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded; the only record of support is the single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: Would lose all timber harvesting on national forests and other federal lands. The bill's findings argue the industry profits from publicly owned resources at unaccounted-for public expense while citizens bear the cost in water quality and lost habitat [S2][S3].

Would lose all access to minerals on some 650 million acres of federal land, including BLM holdings open under the Mining Law. Mining on public land can leave cleanup costs and water pollution with taxpayers [S3].
Would lose all leasing and drilling on federal lands, removing a source of below-market energy leases on publicly owned resources [S3].
Grazing on federal lands would be banned outright, ending a below-market forage subsidy to livestock operators on BLM and Forest Service land [S3].
New motorized trails and recreation developments would be prohibited and non-essential existing roads obliterated, shrinking access for ATV and off-highway-vehicle users [S2][S3].
